opus-5.5.text:
So the way I think about it is that almost every interesting problem in automated reasoning is undecidable or, at best, intractable in the worst case. Whether a program terminates, whether an access-control policy can ever grant a particular permission, whether a cryptographic protocol leaks a key: in theory these are horribly hard. Yet the tools work remarkably well in practice. The question is why, and a big part of the answer is that the search is guided by heuristics, and heuristics are essentially learned knowledge about where to look.

If you look inside a modern SAT solver, conflict-driven clause learning is right there in the name. When the solver hits a contradiction it analyzes why, learns a new clause, and uses it to prune huge parts of the space it would otherwise have explored. Variable selection heuristics like VSIDS are a kind of online learning too. They adapt to the problem in front of them. So learning has been at the heart of making these searches tractable for decades. It just wasn't called machine learning.

What's changing now is that we can bring learning in from the outside as well. Large language models and other learned systems are very good at guessing. They can propose a loop invariant, a ranking function for a termination proof, a lemma, a tactic in an interactive theorem prover, or a decomposition of a big proof into smaller pieces. Historically, finding those creative steps was the hard part, and it's often where a human expert had to step in. Now a model can make a plausible suggestion, and the reasoning engine can check it soundly. If the guess is wrong, you get a counterexample or a failed proof obligation, and you can feed that back and try again.

That division of labor is the important part. The learned component does the intuition, the reasoning component provides the guarantee. You don't have to trust the neural network, because nothing it says is accepted without a proof that a small, trusted checker can verify. That lets you be very aggressive with the heuristic side, because soundness never depends on it.

There's a virtuous cycle here too. The proofs and counterexamples that come out of the reasoning tools are ideal training data. They're precise, they're labeled, and they're correct by construction. So you can use automated reasoning to generate data that makes the learned models better at guessing, and you can use the better models to make the reasoning tools reach further. At AWS we've seen this in practice, in things like policy analysis and in checking the outputs of generative AI against formalized rules. The combination gets you places neither approach reaches alone.

So I don't see learning and reasoning as competitors. Learning is how you make the search tractable. Reasoning is how you know the answer is actually right.

r001.rationale: The response says that when a SAT solver hits a contradiction, it analyzes why, learns a clause, and uses it to prune parts of the search space.

r002.rationale: The response describes retaining learned clauses and adapting heuristics, but does not say that solvers restart from the beginning while retaining lessons from earlier exploration.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, and I think the honest answer is that it's been central to the whole enterprise for longer than people realize, it's just that we didn't always call it learning.

If you look at what a SAT solver does, or an SMT solver, the fundamental problem is that you're searching through this enormous, exponential space. And the naive search is hopeless. What made these tools practical was things like conflict-driven clause learning, where the solver hits a contradiction, analyzes why it got there, and learns a clause that says "don't go down that road again." That's learning. It's not statistical learning, it's logical learning, but the solver is genuinely getting smarter about the specific problem as it goes. And the same thing shows up in the heuristics for which variable to branch on next, which are essentially adaptive, they're keeping score based on what's been useful recently. So the tractability of modern automated reasoning really rests on the solver learning from its own failures.

Then there's the other side, which is where you'd traditionally think of machine learning. The reasoning engines have a lot of knobs, a lot of strategy choices, and which strategy works depends enormously on the shape of the problem. So you can learn, from a corpus of problems, which configuration to try first. Portfolio approaches, algorithm selection, that kind of thing. And that's been quite effective, because the cost of a bad guess is you time out, and the cost of a good guess is you're done in milliseconds.

The thing I find most interesting right now is using learning for the parts that were always the human bottleneck. In program verification, the solver is fine at checking a proof, but somebody has to come up with the invariant, or the ranking function, or the lemma that unlocks the whole thing. That's the creative step. And it turns out that's a very natural place for a model to guess, because a guess is cheap to check. If the neural system proposes an invariant and the symbolic system says no, you've lost nothing except a bit of time. If it says yes, you have a proof that's as trustworthy as any proof ever was.

And that's the framing I keep coming back to. Learning is good at proposing and bad at guaranteeing. Automated reasoning is good at guaranteeing and historically bad at proposing. So the right division of labor is to let the learned component do the searching, the guessing, the prioritization, and keep the symbolic engine as the arbiter of what's actually true. You never have to trust the model. You just have to trust the checker, and the checker is something we've spent decades getting right.

r001.rationale: The response says conflict-driven clause learning analyzes contradictions and learns clauses to avoid those paths again, explaining how lessons from failures prune search.

r002.rationale: The response does not state that a solver restarts from the beginning while retaining lessons from earlier exploration.

astra-6.text:
I think learning has a really important role in guiding the search. In automated reasoning, you often know precisely what constitutes a correct answer, but the space of possible proofs is enormous. The challenge is deciding where to look: which lemma to try, which case to split on, which fact to use next.

Learning can help make those choices. You can learn from previous successful proofs, or from the behavior of the search itself, and use that information to prioritize promising directions. A poor choice might waste time, but it doesn’t have to compromise correctness, because the reasoning engine still checks the proof.

That’s a very attractive combination: learning gives you a way to make informed guesses about how to proceed, and automated reasoning gives you a way to establish that the result is actually right.

r001.rationale: The response says learning can prioritize promising directions, but it does not explain learning root causes of failures or using them to prune the search space.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention restarting the search from the beginning while retaining lessons from earlier exploration.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of learning as a way of guiding the search. In automated reasoning, you often have a very large space of possible proofs, and the challenge is deciding where to look next. Which fact should you use? Which case should you split on? What intermediate assertion might help?

Learning can help make those choices based on what has worked before. The nice thing is that you can separate finding a proof from checking it. A learned system can suggest a step, and the reasoning engine can check whether that step is valid. If the suggestion is wrong, you haven't compromised the correctness of the result—you may just have spent some time looking in an unhelpful direction.

So there's a useful complementary relationship: learning helps you navigate the search space, while automated reasoning provides a precise way to validate what you find.

r001.rationale: The response says learning can guide search based on what worked before, but it does not explain learning root causes of exploration failures to prune the search space.
